newsitem.title: INDIA: Strike hits Indian telecom, postal services.
newsitem.headline: Strike hits Indian telecom, postal services.

text.p: About one million Indian telephone and postal workers launched a nationwide strike over a wage dispute on Wednesday, partially disrupting operations in the country's financial markets.
"According to information reaching us most of the post offices are closed and work has been badly affected," said a senior postal department official who asked not to be identified.
"The strike has paralysed almost 80 to 90 percent of the work across the country, including Delhi," he said.
But the government said telecommunications were likely to be hit less severely.
"Things are normal to the extent that automatic exchanges are not affected," a telephone department official told Reuters.
In Bombay, the nation's financial centre, stock markets were unaffected by the strike but some banks were hit, dealers said.

They said the strike, which affected local phone lines, hit trading in the interbank call money and securities markets and pushed up borrowing rates. Call money rates rose to 10 percent in the afternoon from 8.75 percent at the start, dealers said.

Mallikarjun (one name), secretary-general of the Bharatiya (Indian) Telecom Employees Federation, told Reuters in New Delhi that striking workers were demanding the abolition of a ceiling imposed by the government on annual bonus payments.
Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma told a news conference the government sympathised with workers' demands but called the strike illegal.
"It's an illegal strike as they did not even give a 14-day notice to the government (under the law)," Varma said.
New Delhi normally pays most junior employees an annual bonus during the Hindu festive season in October. The bonus is usually higher than the previous year.
The government this year decided not to raise the payment for its telecommunication and postal employees as part of an austerity programme.
Mallikarjun said the employees were upset because the government had increased the bonus allowance for railway workers but left out the telecommunications sector.

"I am sympathetic to them and our efforts are fully in the direction that our employees should not have any step-motherly treatment compared to other departments. I am committed to avoid injustice," Varma said in a written appeal to the workers.
But Pradip Bhatnagar, a senior official said bonus payments were linked to productivity, which differed between departments.
Mallikarjun said the strike was total. "Now the ball is in their court. Let the government decide and consider the demands of post and telegraph workers," he said.
In June last year, Indian authorities called out troops to restore disrupted telephone services during a five-day strike by about 450,000 telecommunications workers.
The strike had been in protest against the government's moves to end a state monopoly on telephones.
